newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia sets wage arrears payout as protest looms.
newsitem.headline: Russia sets wage arrears payout as protest looms.

text.p: The Russian government said on Tuesday it was working round the clock to complete a cabinet reshuffle and deal with trade union demands before a day of protest which unions expect to draw 20 million Russians.
Government spokesman Igor Shabdurasulov said officials were working intensively to address trade union demands for payment of wage and pension arrears and finalise government changes.

"In the last two weeks, large parts of the government have worked round-the-clock in connection with the reorganisation of the government and the union protests on March 27," he told a news conference.

Trade union leaders said they expected more than 20 million people nationwide, including seven million strikers, to participate in Thursday's planned pickets, rallies and marches to protest against chronic wage arrears.
Workers are owed over 50 trillion roubles ($8.8 billion) in back wages, of which the state owes 10 trillion.

The government said it would unveil its latest plans on Wednesday afternoon at a news conference by a troika of top officials, Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, and Deputy Prime Ministers Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov.
Chubais and Nemtsov are the two most prominent appointees to the new government. Both have pledged to speed up economic reform and Nemtsov has promised to restructure powerful Russian monopolies.
Russia cannot immediately pay off all its debts, but it can detail its approach to the problem of unpaid wages and pensions.

"I wouldn't expect any revolutionary decisions in the next 3-5 days, two weeks, or even month on issues such as natural monopolies, social issues or other problems," Shabdurasulov said. "It's not real to imagine solving such a series of problems tomorrow or the day after tomorrow."
He said it was absurd to hope that all back wages could be paid before Thursday, but said a timetable was being organised to set out realistic goals.
Back pensions would be paid by the end of June, debts to teachers by May, and government debts by the autumn.
It remained unclear to what extent Thursday's day-long protest would succeed, but Shabdurasulov said a small number of groups were ready to mar the event with violence.
Organisers said they had taken special security measures to maintain order. Previous efforts at organised protest have often failed to attract many people to the streets.
Grigory Yavlinsky, head of the liberal Yabloko political party, told journalists he hoped Russians would support the protest actions to show their disapproval of government policy.
While grappling with domestic problems, Russia's political leaders have also been busy on the diplomatic front with meetings with senior officials from China and India.
President Boris Yeltsin met Indian Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda in the Kremlin on Tuesday and said Moscow was committed to maintaining close relations with New Delhi.
"We have been friends for many decades and we remain friends," Yeltsin said. "India remains a stabilising force in its region."
Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen, who came to prepare a visit by Chinese President Ziang Zemin planned for late April, met Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov.

Deve Gowda and Qian are visiting Moscow days after Yeltsin and Clinton "agreed to disagree" at their meeting in the Finnish capital Helsinki over NATO's plans to invite former Soviet bloc states in eastern Europe to join the Western defence alliance.
